name: Margany
confidence_why: Breen's 1981 description of Margany, the only dedicated account of the language, puts main stress on the first vowel of the word with long non-initial vowels sometimes drawing an apparent stress, and the only other source, Holmer's 1983 regional survey, says nothing about Margany stress in particular but only that stress is "not significant" in any of the languages he surveyed with the second syllable often carrying more prominence in longer words, a blanket remark too general and too thinly based to unseat Breen.
catalog_citation: Breen, J.G. (1981). Margany and Gunya. In R.M.W. Dixon & B.J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, Vol. 2, 274-393. Canberra: ANU Press / Amsterdam: John Benjamins. (ANU Open Research scan, hdl 1885/114846)
catalog_locator: section 2.4 'Stress', pp. 295-296 (PDF pages 316-317); Intonation contrast section 2.5, pp. 296-297; consonant symbols per Table 2.1, p. 283
catalog_quote: Main stress is regularly on the first vowel of a word. ... Length in a non-initial vowel (because it is phonemically long or because it is followed by a glide and its homorganic vowel, which sequence may be realised as a diphthong) results in an apparent stress which may sometimes detract from the regular stress on the first vowel, thus [bíyá:lku] /biya:lku/ 'hunt (purposive)'. This is more likely with /a:/ than /i:/ or /u:/ because the latter two are more likely to be realised as two syllables ... There are rare examples in sentences of irregular stress on non-initial vowels but there is not sufficient evidence to justify any further comment on this. ... There may be a secondary stress on the third syllable of a four syllable word especially if the word is a reduplication or a compound form. The third syllable will not be stressed if the second is stressed by virtue of its length ... M…

sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL7091.Q4 H65 1983
sources.quote: 2.11: 'Word or syllable stress is not significant in any of the languages studied here. The spoken context runs smooth without emphasis of any syllable unless in cases of long vowels (or diphthongs) ... however, the second initial syllable often carries mechanically more stress than the others'. 8.5 (Bidjara): 'Neither is word stress [distinctive] ... a certain tendency exists in a spoken context, or in long words, to accentuate the second initial syllable, with secondary stress appearing on subsequent alternate syllables, as in: bibánagana'. Holmer repeats this second-syllable formula for eve
sources.note: Only other primary work with a Marganj chapter; downloaded to check for an independent stress statement -- it has none for Marganj and only a formulaic group-level 'stress not significant / second syllable' remark, so it does not displace Breen 1981.

sources.note: The Margany/Gunya section (pp. 10-11) is entirely about the voiced/voiceless stop contrast, quoted from Breen 1981:283-284 with re-transcribed minimal pairs (kapuny/kabuny, maka/paga, thurti/purdi, thatha/thadha, kuca/kuja; clusters kunkurru/kurn.ga, pintada/pindata). Nothing on Margany word stress, secondary stress, weight, domain or tone. The catalog entry (weight-hedged, vowel-length weight, from Breen 1981) is neither confirmed nor contradicted.
